extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media/political economy, journalists, media critics, activists
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for analyzing mass-media bias and news production that identifies systemic 'filters' and mechanisms (ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, ideology) which shape what becomes news and how it is presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five news 'filters' (the propaganda model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential ingredients of our propaganda model, or set of news 'filters,' fall under the following headings: (I) the size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of the dominant mass-media firms; (2) advertising as the primary income source of the mass media; (3) the reliance of the media on information provided by government, business, and 'experts' funded and approved by these primary sources and agents of power; (4) 'flak' as a means of disciplining the media; and (5) 'anticommunism' as a national religion and control mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the five filters as a checklist for systemic constraints on news: examine ownership/size, revenue model (advertising), sourcing patterns, organized negative responses (flak), and dominant ideological frameworks (anticommunism). The filters interact and produce a 'cleansed residue' of news fit to print; apply a macro (system-level) view alongside story-level analysis to detect their effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size, ownership, and profit orientation of the mass media (first filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The limitation on ownership of media with any substantial outreach by the requisite large size of investment; concentration in a top tier of large, profit-seeking corporations owned/controlled by very wealthy people or managers subject to owners, stockholders, directors, and bankers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess concentration (top-tier companies), ownership structure (family-controlled vs widely held), cross-ownership and diversification, asset/profit scales, and board linkages to corporate/banking elites. Examples: the 'twenty-four media giants' that define the national agenda; GE and Westinghouse ownership ties to non-media industries. Look for pressures to prioritize profitability and to placate investors that shape editorial priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as the primary income source (second filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising functions as the 'license to do business'—advertisers' preferences and discrimination influence which media prosper and what content is produced; advertisers prefer audiences with buying power and avoid sponsoring serious critiques of corporate activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how dependence on advertising affects content: check for programming tailored to 'audience quality' (affluent demographics), avoidance of controversial or investigative programs that 'offend powerful advertisers', and the economic exclusion of ad-disadvantaged outlets (historical example: Daily Herald's decline due to lack of advertising). Use advertiser behavior (sponsorship patterns, client audience profiling) to explain selection and suppression of topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on government, corporate and approved 'experts' for sourcing (third filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The media rely on a steady, reliable flow of raw material provided by government, corporate, and bureaucratic sources and on 'experts' funded/approved by those sources; reporters are predisposed to treat bureaucratic accounts as factual ('principle of bureaucratic affinity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate sourcing patterns: frequency of reliance on official press releases, briefings, wire services, and institutional sources versus independent/dissenting sources. Examine resource-driven choices (daily deadlines, cost of investigative reporting) and the credibility attributed to official sources. Examples: vast Pentagon public-information operations dwarfing dissenting NGOs; routine beats (White House, Pentagon, police) shape who is heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flak as a disciplining mechanism (fourth filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Flak'—negative responses to media statements (letters, complaints, lawsuits, political pressure, advertiser withdrawal, organized criticism)—operates as a means of disciplining the media and steering coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify organized sources of flak (government agencies, corporations, right-wing 'flak machines', advertisers) and document instances where flak led to self-censorship, program sanitization, or withdrawal of funding (example: Gulf + Western withdrawing support from WNET after 'Hungry for Profit'). Measure the presence and potency of flak to explain why certain stories are marginalized or avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-communism (or dominant ideology) as a national religion/control mechanism (fifth filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Anticommunism' is treated as a dominant religion and ideological framework that helps mobilize the populace against enemies and can be used to discredit or marginalize domestic critics and social movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for framing that dichotomizes actors as 'enemy' or 'worthy' based on ideological alignment, and for lowered evidentiary standards when claims fit the dominant ideology. Examples: differential treatment of victims in Poland (worthy) vs Turkey (unworthy); historical Red Scares used to suppress labor and progressive movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-tier centralization and agenda-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: A top tier of 10–24 major media systems (networks, leading newspapers, magazines, syndicators) define the national agenda and supply national/international news to lower-tier outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the hierarchy of sources: which outlets comprise the top tier, how they interlock across media (newspapers, TV, magazines), and how their output is syndicated downward. Analyze how national network centralization (three TV networks historically) concentrates influence and shapes what lower-tier and local media cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource asymmetry between establishment/public-relations operations and dissenting groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishment actors (government, large corporations) possess vastly greater PR resources and institutional capacities to produce and distribute favorable material than dissenting NGOs, church groups, or small advocacy organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify and compare information-production capacities (budgets, staff, press releases, film clips, media services). Use concrete comparisons (e.g., Pentagon's thousands of releases and hundreds of employees vs AFSC/NCC budgets and limited outputs) to explain why establishment narratives dominate coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience 'quality' selection driven by advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Media emphasize attracting audiences with buying power rather than audiences per se; advertisers' measures of audience 'quality' (not just size) shape programming and editorial choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how audience segmentation (Nielsen ratings, Client Audience Profile tools) influences content decisions and why programming that appeals to affluent consumers is privileged. Assess claims that mass-media democracy is akin to a 'voting system weighted by income.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda campaigns and systematic dichotomization of victims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story is 'useful' to elites, government and media can mobilize sustained propaganda campaigns (leaks, press conferences, feature articles) to push an interpretation; conversely, massive victimization that does not serve elite interests will be suppressed or marginalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how campaigns are initiated (government leaks, major outlets starting a theme) and how allied media repeat and amplify the narrative until it becomes accepted truth (examples: KAL 007, campaign coverage of Cambodia/Pol Pot, attacks on Nicaragua). Compare coverage volume and quality for 'worthy' vs 'unworthy' victims and note how utility to elite interests predicts mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement, headlining, tone, and humanization as indicators of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality and prominence of coverage—placement, headlining, word usage, humanizing detail, contextual fullness—systematically differ between favored (worthy) and unfavored (unworthy) subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate story placement, headlines, use of emotionalizing language, depth of humanization, and contextual background. Expect favored victims to be prominently featured, humanized, and provided with fuller context; unfavored victims receive minimal detail and lack contextualization that would generate sympathy or outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and regulatory pressures push media toward profitability and conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Takeovers, takeover threats, investor pressures, deregulation (loosening rules on concentration, cross-ownership, relaxation of 'fairness' constraints) and the attractiveness of media stocks encourage managements to prioritize profitability and align with market-friendly policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of debt-financed expansion, pressure from institutional investors, changes following deregulation, and shifts in programming/policy that reduce perceived regulatory risk. Consider how these financial/market incentives narrow acceptable editorial positions and increase susceptibility to corporate and investor influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on 'experts' and approved intellectual authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Media rely on 'experts' who are funded or approved by government or corporate sources; these experts function as credible purveyors of authoritative accounts that fit establishment frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which experts are repeatedly cited, their institutional affiliations and funding, and how their authority is invoked to legitimize official narratives. Watch for the elevation of defectors or ideologues when they serve anti-enemy purposes regardless of evidential quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a macro (system-level) alongside micro (story-level) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To perceive manipulation and systematic bias it 'requires a macro, alongside a micro- (story-by-story), view of media operations'—systemic forces set the premises within which individual journalists operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating coverage, combine structural analysis (ownership, revenue, sourcing regimes, ideology) with close readings of individual stories to see how filters shape choices, framing, and omissions. Use both levels to explain why professional journalistic integrity may coexist with systemic bias.
